sections.title: Why this module matters
sections.body: gRPC is the dominant inter-service communication protocol in Go microservice architectures, used by Google, Lyft, Netflix, and most cloud-native Go shops. It provides a contract-first, binary-encoded, bidirectional-streaming RPC framework on top of HTTP/2. Interviewers evaluate this module to check whether you understand the four RPC modes, how to write and register interceptors (the gRPC equivalent of HTTP middleware), how Protobuf encoding differs from JSON, and when to favour gRPC over REST. Knowing the streaming patterns in detail — especially their error propagation and cancellation semantics — demonstrates senior-level gRPC experience.

sections.title: Mental model
sections.body: A .proto file is the source of truth: it defines service methods and message types. protoc with the grpc-go plugin generates two files — *.pb.go (message types) and *_grpc.pb.go (server/client interfaces). Your server struct embeds UnimplementedXxxServer and overrides only the methods it needs. grpc.NewServer() with option lists (credentials, interceptors, keepalive) creates the server; you register your implementation with pb.RegisterXxxServer, then listen on a TCP port. Client stubs are created with grpc.Dial (or grpc.NewClient in newer versions) and a connection object is shared across all RPC calls — it manages a pool of HTTP/2 streams internally. Interceptors (UnaryInterceptor, StreamInterceptor) wrap all RPC calls for auth, logging, and tracing without modifying individual handler methods.

sections.title: Must-know concepts
sections.body: 1. Four RPC types — Unary (req/resp), Server Streaming (req/stream of resp), Client Streaming (stream of req/resp), Bidirectional Streaming (stream/stream). 2. Protobuf field numbers — immutable wire identifiers; never reuse a deleted field number; add new optional fields freely. 3. grpc.Status error codes — always return status.Errorf(codes.NotFound, ...) not raw errors; clients receive the code and message. 4. Context propagation — gRPC passes metadata (headers) via context; use metadata.NewOutgoingContext on the client and metadata.FromIncomingContext on the server. 5. Unary interceptor signature — func(ctx, req, info *UnaryServerInfo, handler UnaryHandler) (interface{}, error) — chain multiple with grpc_middleware.ChainUnaryServer. 6. Stream interceptor — wraps the ServerStream interface; override SendMsg/RecvMsg for logging. 7. keepalive.ServerParameters / ClientParameters — prevent idle connections from being killed by network intermediaries. 8. grpc-gateway — generates a reverse proxy that translates HTTP/JSON to gRPC; lets you serve both protocols from one server.

sections.title: Likely interview hooks
sections.body: Q: What are the four gRPC communication modes and when would you use each? — Unary for standard request/response; server streaming for large result sets (search results, logs); client streaming for batch uploads; bidirectional for real-time two-way communication like a chat or live dashboard. Q: How do you implement authentication in gRPC? — Write a unary interceptor that extracts the Authorization metadata key, validates the JWT, and injects the claims into the context; or use per-RPC credentials on the client side. Q: Why does Protobuf use field numbers instead of field names on the wire? — Field numbers are encoded as varints (1-3 bytes for small numbers), making the binary payload much smaller than JSON with string keys; they are stable across renames. Q: What is grpc-gateway and why would you use it? — It generates an HTTP/JSON reverse proxy from proto annotations, so the same gRPC service serves browser clients and external partners without maintaining a separate REST API. Q: How do you cancel a server-streaming RPC from the client? — Call the context cancel function; the server checks ctx.Done() in its send loop and stops streaming.

sections.title: Speaking template
sections.body: "In our microservice platform all internal service-to-service calls use gRPC because the contract-first proto file acts as a living API specification, Protobuf encoding is 3-5x smaller than JSON for our message shapes, and HTTP/2 multiplexing means we get parallel streams over a single connection. I define the service in a .proto file, check it into a shared repo, and use buf lint and buf breaking to catch backward-incompatible changes in CI. For cross-cutting concerns — auth, request IDs, error normalisation, tracing spans — I chain unary and stream interceptors rather than embedding logic in handlers. For external-facing APIs where browser clients need to connect, I use grpc-gateway to expose an HTTP/JSON facade, which means I maintain one proto definition and get both protocols for free."
